title: Tropical and monsoon fevers
summary: Monsoon and tropical fevers that fill Indian ICUs: a syndromic approach to acute febrile illness with empirical cover, then severe malaria, severe dengue, leptospirosis, scrub typhus and enteric fever, each with Indian national and WHO guidance.

topics.title: Approach to severe acute febrile illness
topics.summary: In the monsoon, a febrile patient with thrombocytopenia, jaundice, AKI or ARDS could have malaria, dengue, leptospirosis, scrub typhus or enteric fever, alone or together. Send the core tests, then start empirical ceftriaxone plus doxycycline (or azithromycin), with artesunate if malaria is not yet excluded.

steps.title: Bedside
steps.detail: Eschar (groin, axilla, under breasts/waistband): scrub typhus. Conjunctival suffusion, calf tenderness, flood/sewage exposure: leptospirosis. Rash, retro-orbital pain, rising haematocrit: dengue. Travel/endemic zone, rigors: malaria. Step-ladder fever, relative bradycardia: enteric.

steps.title: Core panel
steps.detail: Peripheral smear + malaria RDT (repeat if negative), dengue NS1 (days 1-5)/IgM (after day 5), scrub typhus IgM ELISA, leptospira IgM, blood cultures ×2, CBC with haematocrit, LFT, creatinine, lactate, urine, CXR.

steps.title: Severe AFI
steps.detail: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily + doxycycline 100 mg 12-hourly (azithromycin in pregnancy). Add IV artesunate if smear/RDT unavailable or pending in an endemic area.

steps.title: Common patterns
steps.detail: ARDS (scrub, lepto, falciparum), AKI (lepto, falciparum), shock (dengue leakage vs septic), encephalopathy (cerebral malaria, scrub, JE), bleeding (dengue, lepto).

steps.title: 48-72 h
steps.detail: Narrow therapy once a diagnosis is confirmed; consider co-infection (up to 10-15% in some series) if not improving.

tables.title: Distinguishing features of tropical fevers
rows: Endemic area, rigors, coma, jaundice, AKI
Retro-orbital pain, rash, defervescence day 3-7 then shock
Water/sewage exposure, calf pain, conjunctival suffusion
Non-oliguric hypokalaemic AKI, high bilirubin with modest ALT, high CPK
Step-ladder fever, abdominal pain, relative bradycardia
Normal/low WBC, blood culture positive in week 1
tables.caption: Overlap is the rule; empirical dual cover is justified in severe disease until results return.

redFlags.text: Fever with altered sensorium, shock, SpO2 < 92% or bleeding: ICU-level care.

pitfalls.text: A single negative smear does not exclude malaria; repeat 12-24 hourly ×3.
Labelling all fever with thrombocytopenia as dengue and missing scrub typhus or malaria.

pearls.text: Look for the eschar under clothing: painless, black, often in skin folds.

nodes.text: Smear/RDT, NS1/IgM, scrub/lepto IgM, cultures, lactate
Reassess: co-infection, other sepsis source, HLH

consultantNotes.evidence: - **ISCCM 2014 tropical fevers guideline** and **ICMR 2019 treatment guidelines**: syndromic approach, tests and empirical regimens.
consultantNotes.controversies: - Routine empirical doxycycline in all AFI vs test-and-treat depends on local scrub typhus prevalence.
consultantNotes.indiaNotes: - Seasonal peaks July-November; regional patterns: scrub typhus in hilly and southern states, leptospirosis in coastal Maharashtra, Kerala, Gujarat; falciparum in Odisha, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand and the north-east.

topics.title: Severe malaria
topics.summary: Any severity criterion with asexual parasites (P. falciparum, and also P. vivax or knowlesi) = severe malaria: IV artesunate 2.4 mg/kg at 0, 12, 24 h then daily, followed by a full oral ACT course, plus glucose monitoring, careful fluids, and organ support.

steps.title: Smear + RDT
steps.detail: Parasite count; but treat on clinical grounds if testing is delayed.

steps.title: Artesunate
steps.detail: 2.4 mg/kg IV (or IM) at 0, 12, 24 h, then daily until oral intake (≥ 24 h), then complete 3-day ACT (+ single-dose primaquine for falciparum per national policy).

steps.title: Hourly-4 hourly
steps.detail: Hypoglycaemia (< 40 mg/dL) is common, especially in pregnancy and with quinine; give dextrose.

steps.title: Restrictive
steps.detail: No aggressive boluses (FEAST-type harm; ARDS risk); treat hypovolaemia cautiously; early RRT for AKI or severe acidosis.

steps.title: Supportive
steps.detail: Transfuse if Hb < 7 g/dL; antibiotics if shock or suspected bacteraemia; treat seizures; no steroids, mannitol or exchange transfusion.

steps.title: Late haemolysis
steps.detail: Hb at day 7, 14 and 28 after artesunate (PADH). Vivax: G6PD test, then primaquine 0.25 mg/kg daily × 14 days for radical cure.

doseCards.dose: 2.4 mg/kg at 0, 12, 24 h, then every 24 h
doseCards.workedExample: 55 kg: 132 mg ≈ 2.2 vials (60 mg); reconstitute each vial with 1 mL bicarbonate + 5 mL saline (10 mg/mL) → 13.2 mL IV

tables.title: WHO criteria for severe malaria (adults; any one with parasitaemia)
rows: Base deficit > 8, HCO3- < 15 mmol/L or lactate ≥ 5 mmol/L
Radiological, or SpO2 < 92% on air with RR > 30
Recurrent/prolonged nose, gum or venepuncture bleeding, haematemesis, melaena
tables.caption: From WHO severe malaria definitions (WHO malaria guidelines).

redFlags.text: Pregnant woman with falciparum malaria: high risk of hypoglycaemia, pulmonary oedema and fetal loss; artesunate in all trimesters.

pitfalls.text: Using quinine when artesunate is available (higher mortality).
Liberal fluid boluses precipitating pulmonary oedema.
Ignoring severe vivax malaria (ARDS, AKI, thrombocytopenia occur in India).

pearls.text: Artesunate reduced mortality vs quinine by 35% in Asian adults (SEAQUAMAT) and 22.5% in African children (AQUAMAT).

nodes.text: Glucose checks; cautious fluids; transfuse Hb < 7
Full 3-day ACT + primaquine per policy; Hb days 7/14/28

consultantNotes.evidence:
- **SEAQUAMAT 2005:** mortality 15% artesunate vs 22% quinine in adults.
- **AQUAMAT 2010:** 8.5% vs 10.9% in African children.
consultantNotes.indiaNotes: - Artesunate is supplied by the national programme; severe vivax malaria and mixed infections are increasingly reported. ACT choice differs: AS+SP nationally, artemether-lumefantrine in the north-east.

topics.title: Severe dengue and dengue shock
topics.summary: Plasma leakage peaks in the critical phase around defervescence (days 3-7). Guide crystalloid by haematocrit, capillary refill, lactate and urine output; step fluids down quickly; avoid prophylactic platelets; and recognise reabsorption-phase overload.

steps.title: Know the timeline
steps.detail: Febrile (days 1-3), critical (around defervescence, 24-48 h of leakage), recovery (reabsorption; fluid overload risk).

steps.title: Admit
steps.detail: Abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, fluid accumulation, mucosal bleeding, lethargy, liver > 2 cm, rising haematocrit with falling platelets.

steps.title: Fluids
steps.detail: Crystalloid 5-7 mL/kg/h for 1-2 h, then 3-5 mL/kg/h for 2-4 h, then 2-3 mL/kg/h, adjusted to haematocrit and clinical response.

steps.title: 5-10 mL/kg/h
steps.detail: Crystalloid 5-10 mL/kg over 1 h; if improving, step down to 5-7, 3-5, 2-3 mL/kg/h over 24-48 h.

steps.title: Bolus
steps.detail: 20 mL/kg crystalloid over 15-30 min; repeat; if haematocrit falls with persistent shock, suspect occult bleeding and transfuse blood. Guide with capillary refill time and lactate.

steps.title: Only for bleeding
steps.detail: Prophylactic platelet transfusion does not reduce bleeding (Lye 2017); transfuse for significant bleeding or procedures.

steps.title: Harmful
steps.detail: NSAIDs and aspirin, IM injections, steroids, immunoglobulins; minimise invasive procedures.

tables.title: Crystalloid step-down in compensated dengue shock (adult)
tables.caption: Reassess at each step: vital signs, CRT, haematocrit, urine output (target ~0.5 mL/kg/h). If not improving, check haematocrit: rising → more crystalloid/colloid; falling → bleeding, transfuse.

redFlags.text: Narrow pulse pressure (≤ 20 mmHg) with normal systolic BP: compensated shock.
Shock with falling haematocrit: internal bleeding.
Breathlessness with effusions after day 7: reabsorption overload; stop IV fluid, consider diuretic.

pitfalls.text: Treating the platelet count rather than the patient.
Continuing IV fluids at a high rate after leakage stops.

pearls.text: Haematocrit rise ≥ 20% from baseline signals significant leakage.

consultantNotes.evidence:
- **WHO 2009 dengue guideline:** phase-based fluid protocols.
- **WHO 2025 arboviral guideline:** crystalloids over colloids; CRT and lactate to guide fluids; against NSAIDs, steroids and immunoglobulins.
- **Lye 2017:** prophylactic platelets did not reduce bleeding and caused more adverse events.
consultantNotes.indiaNotes: - India reports hundreds of thousands of dengue cases yearly; platelet transfusion demand driven by counts is a major waste of blood products.

topics.title: Leptospirosis (Weil's disease)
topics.summary: After flood or sewage exposure: fever, myalgia, conjunctival suffusion, then jaundice, non-oliguric hypokalaemic AKI, pulmonary haemorrhage and myocarditis. Give penicillin G or ceftriaxone early; dialyse early; lung-protective ventilation for pulmonary haemorrhage.

steps.title: Exposure
steps.detail: Wading in flood water, farming (paddy), sewer work, animal contact, 2-20 days before.

steps.title: Weil's
steps.detail: Jaundice with modest transaminase rise, AKI (often non-oliguric with hypokalaemia), thrombocytopenia, haemoptysis/pulmonary haemorrhage, myocarditis, aseptic meningitis.

steps.title: Tests
steps.detail: IgM ELISA (after day 5), MAT (reference), PCR in first week; do not wait for results to treat.

steps.title: Antibiotics
steps.detail: Penicillin G 1.5 MU IV 6-hourly or ceftriaxone 1-2 g IV daily for 7 days; doxycycline 100 mg 12-hourly for milder disease.

steps.title: Kidney and lung
steps.detail: Replace K+; early daily dialysis for oliguria, hyperkalaemia, acidosis or overload; pulmonary haemorrhage: intubation, low tidal volume, high PEEP; consider plasma exchange or steroids only in trials/selected cases.

doseCards.dose: 1.5 million units every 6 h for 7 days

redFlags.text: New haemoptysis or falling Hb with infiltrates: pulmonary haemorrhage; high mortality; intubate early.

pitfalls.text: Missing hypokalaemia in polyuric leptospiral AKI.

pearls.text: Bilirubin very high with only modestly raised ALT and high CPK points to leptospirosis rather than viral hepatitis.

nodes.text: Jaundice, AKI, bleeding or lung involvement?
Early intubation, lung-protective ventilation, high PEEP
K+ replacement; early dialysis if needed

consultantNotes.evidence: - **WHO 2003 guidance** for diagnosis; antibiotic choice from ICMR 2019 and ISCCM 2014.
consultantNotes.controversies: - Benefit of antibiotics late in disease and of steroids/plasma exchange for pulmonary haemorrhage is uncertain.
consultantNotes.indiaNotes: - Outbreaks follow monsoon floods in Mumbai, Kerala, Gujarat, coastal Karnataka and the Andaman Islands.

topics.title: Scrub typhus
topics.summary: Orientia tsutsugamushi infection with fever, eschar and lymphadenopathy that can progress to ARDS, AKI, shock, myocarditis and meningoencephalitis. Severe disease: IV doxycycline plus azithromycin for 7 days (INTREST).

steps.title: Clues
steps.detail: Rural/bush/farm exposure, eschar (present in ~50% of Indian cases), regional lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, ALT > AST, thrombocytopenia, ARDS.

steps.title: IgM ELISA
steps.detail: IgM ELISA is the mainstay; IFA is gold standard; Weil-Felix is specific but insensitive; PCR of eschar or blood early.

steps.title: Non-severe
steps.detail: Doxycycline 100 mg 12-hourly for 7 days; azithromycin 500 mg daily in pregnancy and children.

steps.title: Severe
steps.detail: IV doxycycline + IV azithromycin for 7 days: INTREST composite of death, persistent complications or fever at day 7: 33% combination vs 47% doxycycline vs 48% azithromycin.

steps.title: Organs
steps.detail: Lung-protective ventilation for ARDS; RRT; vasopressors; meningoencephalitis care; monitor for myocarditis and conduction defects.

doseCards.dose: 200 mg load, then 100 mg every 12 h for 7 days
doseCards.verify: INTREST used IV doxycycline 200 mg loading dose followed by 100 mg twice daily; confirm against the trial protocol.

doseCards.dose: 1 g on day 1, then 500 mg daily for 7 days

redFlags.text: Hypoxaemia, hypotension, GCS fall or creatinine rising in a febrile patient with eschar: severe scrub typhus; combination IV therapy.

pitfalls.text: Treating with β-lactams alone (no activity against Orientia).

pearls.text: Defervescence within 48 h of doxycycline is so typical that persistent fever should prompt re-evaluation.

consultantNotes.evidence: - **INTREST 2023 (n = 794, India):** combination IV doxycycline + azithromycin reduced the composite primary outcome vs either alone.
consultantNotes.indiaNotes: - Endemic across the "tsutsugamushi triangle"; major cause of AFI and AES in Himachal, Uttarakhand, Tamil Nadu, Andhra, Northeast and Gorakhpur (AES).

topics.title: Enteric fever (typhoid and paratyphoid)
topics.summary: Complicated enteric fever (encephalopathy, shock, perforation, GI bleeding) needs IV ceftriaxone (or azithromycin combination), blood cultures before antibiotics, and early surgical review for perforation. Fluoroquinolone resistance is high in India.

steps.title: Cultures
steps.detail: Blood culture (best in week 1, ~40-80% sensitive); bone marrow culture more sensitive; Widal is unreliable.

steps.title: Uncomplicated
steps.detail: Azithromycin 500 mg-1 g daily for 7 days or cefixime orally; fluoroquinolones only if susceptible.

steps.title: Severe
steps.detail: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily (some use 2 g 12-hourly or 4 g/day in severe cases) for 10-14 days ± azithromycin; adjust to susceptibility. XDR typhoid (travel from Pakistan): meropenem + azithromycin.

steps.title: Week 2-3
steps.detail: Perforation (abdominal pain, guarding, free gas): resuscitate, add anaerobic cover, urgent laparotomy. GI bleed: transfusion, endoscopy. Encephalopathy/shock: consider high-dose dexamethasone (3 mg/kg then 1 mg/kg 6-hourly × 8 doses).

redFlags.text: New abdominal pain and tachycardia in the second week: perforation.

pitfalls.text: Diagnosing typhoid on a single Widal titre.
Ciprofloxacin as empirical therapy in India (high resistance).

pearls.text: Fever often takes 4-7 days to settle even on effective therapy; do not switch antibiotics too early.

nodes.text: Azithromycin or cefixime; tailor to culture
Continue 10-14 days; dexamethasone if severe toxaemia

consultantNotes.evidence:
- **Parry 2002 NEJM review:** clinical features, diagnosis, complications, dexamethasone in severe typhoid (Hoffman 1984).
- **ICMR 2019:** regimen choices and resistance data for India.
consultantNotes.indiaNotes: - Fluoroquinolone non-susceptibility in Salmonella Typhi is very high in India; ceftriaxone MICs are rising. Typhoid conjugate vaccine is being introduced.

drugs.name: Artesunate (IV/IM)
drugs.indications: Severe malaria of any species, all ages, all trimesters of pregnancy.
drugs.adultDose: 2.4 mg/kg IV/IM at 0, 12 and 24 h, then every 24 h until able to take oral (minimum 24 h); then full 3-day oral ACT. Children < 20 kg: 3 mg/kg per dose.
drugs.preparationIndia: 60 mg vial with 1 mL 5% sodium bicarbonate (reconstitute) then 5 mL 0.9% saline/5% dextrose for IV (10 mg/mL). Supplied free through the national programme in many states.
drugs.cautions: Post-artesunate delayed haemolysis (check Hb at days 7, 14, 28).

drugs.name: Ceftriaxone
drugs.indications: Empirical severe AFI; enteric fever; leptospirosis.
drugs.adultDose: 2 g IV once daily (2 g 12-hourly if meningitis suspected).
drugs.cautions: Rising MICs in Salmonella Typhi; biliary sludge.

drugs.name: Doxycycline
drugs.indications: Scrub typhus and other rickettsioses; leptospirosis; empirical AFI cover.
drugs.adultDose: 100 mg orally/IV every 12 h for 7 days (INTREST IV regimen: 200 mg load then 100 mg 12-hourly).
drugs.preparationIndia: Oral widely available; IV doxycycline 100 mg vials have intermittent availability.
drugs.cautions: Avoid in pregnancy (use azithromycin); oesophagitis with oral tablets.
drugs.verify: Confirm IV doxycycline availability and the INTREST loading regimen.

drugs.name: Azithromycin
drugs.indications: Scrub typhus (pregnancy, children, or with doxycycline in severe disease); enteric fever.
drugs.adultDose: Scrub typhus: 500 mg daily IV/oral (INTREST: 1 g day 1 then 500 mg daily) for 5-7 days. Enteric fever: 1 g day 1 then 500 mg daily, or 20 mg/kg/day for 7 days.

drugs.name: Benzylpenicillin (penicillin G)
drugs.adultDose: 1.5 million units IV every 6 h for 7 days.

drugs.name: Primaquine
drugs.indications: Radical cure of P. vivax/ovale; single low dose for P. falciparum gametocytes.
drugs.adultDose: Vivax: 0.25 mg/kg daily for 14 days. Falciparum: 0.75 mg/kg single dose (national programme).
drugs.cautions: Haemolysis in G6PD deficiency; avoid in pregnancy and infants.
